USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Keep existing Section 301 tariffs in place and continue the Washington talks. Do not automatically raise List 3 from 10% to 25% on March 1 while negotiations are still producing movement, and do not trade a purchase-only package or the Meng Wanzhou case for a premature rollback. Any short extension of the truce should be conditioned on written progress on IP, forced technology transfer, industrial subsidies, and a usable enforcement mechanism.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The current state of the dispute is a modest US opportunity, not a high threat. Washington still holds the larger tariff footprint (about $250B of Chinese goods under Section 301 versus China's smaller matching lists) and Beijing is at the table offering purchases after the 1 Dec 2018 G20 pause of the scheduled List 3 hike (timeline 2018-12-01; 2019-01-07; 2019-01-30; 2019-02-14). Risk pricing has eased (VIX 14.02 on 2019-02-20 after the December spike) and the yuan has firmed to about 6.76 rather than breaking weaker, which is consistent with China wanting to avoid a March hike. That leverage justifies a modestly negative threat score of minus 0.25, not an existential or even high threat. It is not a clean opportunity either: US goods exports to China have fallen (about $9.7B in Sep-18 to $8.1B in Feb-19), imports from China have dropped sharply, Michigan sentiment fell from 100.1 to 93.8, and industrial production has slipped. Farm-belt retaliation is the main domestic cost—soy shipments to China collapsed after China's July 2018 25% tariff, USDA aid was required, and only limited buying resumed after Buenos Aires. Action stays near zero (plus 0.05, negotiate) because hiking to 25% now would risk collapsing a live negotiation that Trump has already called a non-magical date, while rolling back or locking in purchases without enforcement would repeat the May 2018 false truce. Huawei/Meng (timeline 2018-12-01, 2019-01-28) should stay on the law-enforcement track, not be bargained into the tariff text.
key_factors: Live Feb 2019 talks: progress on purchases, unresolved IP/tech-transfer/enforcement
US tariff leverage intact: List 3 still at 10% with a threatened hike to 25%
Farm-sector retaliation (soybeans and related) is the main US cost and political constraint
US macro is cooling at the margin (sentiment, IP, bilateral trade) but not in crisis; VIX has normalized
Huawei/Meng raises tech and security stakes and should not be folded into a cheap commercial deal
Trump has signaled March 1 can slide if a real deal is close—use that optionality rather than auto-escalate

sources_cited.excerpt: G20 Buenos Aires dinner: Trump and Xi agree to a 90-day negotiation window. Planned Jan 1, 2019 hike of List 3 from 10% to 25% is suspended (tariffs remain at 10%). Same day: Canada arrests Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou.
Another round of talks (through Feb 15). Progress reported on purchases; enforcement mechanism still disputed.
Lighthizer and Mnuchin in Beijing for high-level talks. Purchase commitments discussed; enforcement and structural IP/tech-transfer issues unresolved.
List 3 takes effect at 10%. Combined US Section 301 coverage now ~$250B of Chinese imports.
US DOJ unseals fraud and sanctions-related charges against Huawei and Meng; US formally requests Meng's extradition from Canada.
University of Michigan consumer sentiment fell from 100.1 (Sep 2018) to 91.2 (Jan 2019) and only partially recovered to 93.8 (Feb 2019).
US goods exports to mainland China declined from $9.73B (Sep 2018) to $8.08B (Feb 2019), about -17% over the window.
US goods imports from China fell from $52.1B (Oct 2018) to $33.0B (Feb 2019), a ~34% drop over the window.
VIX closed 14.02 on 2019-02-20 after peaking at 36.07 on 2018-12-24—risk pricing has normalized during the truce/talks.
CNY strengthened from a weak ~6.97 in late Oct 2018 to 6.756 on 2019-02-19, consistent with China not forcing a devaluation during talks.
As of 20 Feb 2019, Liu He was due in Washington; Trump said March 1 is not a magical date and the real question is whether tariffs rise.
Trump said he could let the March 1 deadline slide if close to a real deal but was not inclined to; structural issues remain the US demand.
US ag exports to China down 42% in first 10 months of 2018 to ~$8.3B; China had been a ~$12B soybean market.
DOJ Huawei/Meng charges landed on the eve of January talks and are entangled with the broader attempt to unwind Chinese tech advantages.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Keep negotiating through the Liu He–Lighthizer/Mnuchin channel and treat the March 1 List-3 hike as the immediate problem to defuse, not a cue to retaliate again. Put concrete purchase volumes (soy, energy, aircraft) on the table as the price of a deadline slide or a standstill at 10%, while refusing a U.S.-run enforcement mechanism that would police industrial policy inside China. Do not add tariffs or further hostage-taking now; do not pre-commit structural rollback of Made in China 2025 or a full tariff climb-down before Washington offers a matching tariff freeze.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is high but not existential. The United States already covers ~$250B of Chinese goods (25% on the $50B Lists 1–2; 10% on List 3), and the G20 truce only paused the scheduled jump of List 3 to 25% on ~$200B (timeline 2018-09-24, 2018-12-01). That hike, if triggered, would hit the same export machine already showing stress: 2018 GDP slowed to 6.6% (three-decade low), Q4 to 6.4%, official manufacturing PMI was still in contraction at 49.5 in January, and December exports fell 4.4%. Firm-level tech targeting is live and distinct from tariffs: the ZTE denial order (2018-04-16), Meng’s arrest the same day as the G20 dinner, and the 2019-01-28 unsealing of Huawei/Meng fraud and sanctions charges plus a formal extradition request. That combination sits near the CHN +0.5 anchor (export sectors + national-champion targeting) but is pulled back from +0.5–+1.0 by mixed near-term data and an open diplomatic window: January dollar exports rose 9.1% (Lunar New Year caveats apply), China–US goods imports into the United States have already collapsed (IMPCH from ~$52.1B in Oct-2018 to ~$33.0B in Feb-2019), and Trump has publicly said March 1 is “not a magical date” and that the deadline could “slide” if a real deal is close. Action should therefore stay on the negotiate band, not escalate. Escalation would make the 25% hike more likely and deepen the export/employment hit China is already trying to offset with stimulus. Full concession or concede_purchases as the headline move is premature: talks have produced purchase progress but no matching U.S. offer to roll back existing 301 tariffs, and Lighthizer is still demanding “enforcement, enforcement, enforcement” plus structural IP/subsidy changes China has not accepted (timeline 2019-01-30, 2019-02-14). Purchases can be used inside the negotiation to buy time and split Trump (who wants a “big deal” and farm-belt wins) from Lighthizer (who rejects a purchases-only outcome). Hold the Meng/Huawei file on a separate legal-political track rather than trading core industrial policy for her release; Trump has already floated politicizing the case, which is leverage, not a reason to fold on sovereignty.
key_factors: Pending March 1 hike of List 3 from 10% to 25% on ~$200B still the binding near-term shock
Existing $250B Section 301 coverage plus Huawei/Meng indictment is the core threat to exports and tech champions
Domestic slowdown is real (2018 GDP 6.6%, PMI <50) but January trade was not a collapse
Talks are live with reported purchase progress and an unresolved enforcement/sovereignty gap
Trump has softened the hard deadline, creating room to negotiate a standstill without new Chinese escalation
No matching U.S. tariff rollback is on the table, so purchases should be bargaining chips inside talks, not a unilateral concession
